rich_summary: This section of the Bhagavad Gita (Chapter IV) presents Krishna explaining the ancient origin and spiritual purpose of his teaching on devotion and action. He describes how the doctrine was passed through royal sages but was lost over time, prompting him to reveal it again to Arjuna. Krishna clarifies his divine nature: though unborn and eternal, he incarnates whenever righteousness declines and injustice rises, protecting the virtuous and restoring moral order. The chapter explores the paradox of action—true wisdom lies in acting without attachment to results. Various forms of sacrifice are described, culminating in the claim that the sacrifice of knowledge is highest because knowledge burns away the bondage of action. Faith, disciplined senses, and guidance from the wise lead to liberating knowledge that destroys doubt and leads to spiritual peace.

highlight_spans.why: Establishes the hierarchy from senses to mind to knowledge and finally the supreme reality, framing the spiritual psychology of the Gita.
Krishna reveals his paradoxical nature—unborn yet incarnating through divine power—introducing the theology of divine avatars.
The famous declaration that Krishna manifests whenever righteousness declines, one of the central doctrinal statements of the Gita.
The paradox of 'seeing inaction in action and action in inaction' captures the core philosophical insight about detached action.
The metaphor of the fire of knowledge burning actions to ashes powerfully expresses liberation through spiritual understanding.

top_scenes.scene_text: Krishna, radiant and calm, reveals his divine nature to Arjuna on the battlefield chariot as the armies of Kurukshetra wait in tense silence.
A symbolic vision of Krishna appearing again and again through the ages whenever darkness and injustice rise in the world.
A sage meditating before a blazing sacrificial fire that transforms into pure light, symbolizing knowledge burning away the bonds of action.
